rows.summary: Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD now. Your own order system shows the tote was never shipped because it was out of stock, so there is nothing to contest, and resolving at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

This is still an inquiry, and your tracking only shows the tote as shipped, not delivered, so contesting now would be weak. Send the buyer the tracking number and a reassuring update, then watch for delivery. If tracking later confirms delivery to the San Jose address, submit it as proof of fulfillment.

Refund the $48.00 in full. The only tracking on file was cancelled, so there is no proof the tote shipped or was delivered. Contesting would almost certainly fail, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation.

Submit proof of fulfillment now. Include the USPS tracking number and the delivery scan showing delivery to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, which is the day after the buyer said they never got it. The PayPal tracker still shows only SHIPPED and the scan was entered by you, so make sure USPS's own tracking page confirms delivery before you submit.

Message the buyer and double-check the tracking number before contesting. The only delivery scan is dated Sep 28, four days before the Oct 2 payment, so it likely belongs to a different shipment and would not persuade PayPal.

You've already submitted tracking and offered $20, and PayPal is waiting on the buyer, so send a short follow-up message rather than acting on the case. PayPal's tracker shows the package only as SHIPPED, not delivered, so don't escalate on the tracking you have; if the buyer won't settle, a full refund may be safer than a claim.

Message the buyer and hold off on contesting. The delivery scan you entered lists ZIP 10001, but the order ships to 95131, so it isn't solid proof of delivery yet; check with USPS while you ask the buyer to look for the package.

Submit the USPS tracking number and its delivery scan as supporting info. The scan shows delivery to the order's San Jose 95131 address on Oct 4, and the transaction is seller-protection eligible, so this item-not-received case is worth defending rather than refunding $75.
Refund the $48.00 in full. The buyer says the tote never arrived, and the only tracking on file is cancelled, so you have no delivery proof that would win this case under PayPal review.

PayPal is reviewing this $48.00 item-not-received case and currently allows no seller action, so there is nothing to submit right now. Outside PayPal, gather carrier tracking showing delivery to the San Jose address so you are ready if PayPal requests information.
Refund the $8.00 in full. Without carrier tracking you cannot prove delivery for an item-not-received case, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.
The buyer has said they found the tote at a neighbor's and would close the case, but it is still open six days later. Send a short, friendly reminder asking them to close it rather than refunding.

Contest with proof of fulfillment: submit the USPS tracking number and the delivery confirmation showing an adult signature from J DOE at the buyer's San Jose ZIP on Oct 5. Attach the official USPS tracking and signature record, since the delivery scan on file was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. The USPS scan shows delivery to the buyer's ship-to ZIP, the buyer admits tracking shows delivered, and the sale is seller-protection eligible; attach the official USPS tracking page for 9400100000000000000011 so PayPal can verify the scan you entered.

Send the buyer a polite message with the tracking number and ask them to check it and wait a few more days. Messaging is the only action PayPal allows on this inquiry, and the tracking shows the tote shipped but not yet delivered.

This is an early-stage item-not-received inquiry with no tracking on file, so contesting now would not persuade PayPal. Message the buyer to confirm the order status and share tracking if you have it. If you can't show delivery, offer or accept before the case escalates.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the USPS tracking number and the delivery scan showing delivery to the buyer's ship-to ZIP on Oct 4. The buyer rejected your $15 offer, and this order is eligible for seller protection. Upload the actual USPS tracking record rather than a typed summary, because PayPal's own tracker only shows SHIPPED.

Message the buyer before taking any formal step. Share that the tote was listed and packed as olive green, which can read as brownish in some light, and invite them to return it or accept a small partial refund. This is an early inquiry, so a friendly resolution now avoids escalation and the dispute fee. A color-perception complaint is hard to win outright.

Refund the $30.00 in full. The buyer reports the mug arrived smashed and uploaded a photo of it cracked through the handle, and there is no evidence on file showing it arrived intact. Settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and the dispute fee.

Offer a 25.00 USD partial refund, the price of the missing tote. Your own packing log confirms only one of the two totes was sent, so contesting would fail, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Message the buyer before taking any PayPal action. Their 'box arrived empty' note (Oct 3) is dated a day before your USPS delivery scan (Oct 4), so they may be describing a different package. PayPal's tracker also shows only SHIPPED, not delivered, which makes contesting now weak.

Reply to the buyer in the PayPal case. Point to the manufacturer authenticity certificate for serial MX-22841 and ask what makes them think the tote is fake, with photos. The case is still an inquiry, and the buyer has given no detail beyond one line, so resolving it in conversation avoids escalation without refunding $450 for an item your records show is authentic.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. The order is eligible for seller protection, and USPS tracking shows delivery to the ship-to address in San Jose. That is usually the key evidence in an unauthorized-transaction case. Submit the tracking number with the delivery confirmation, ideally a screenshot or record pulled straight from USPS, since the delivery scan on file was entered by you.

Your refund log shows a full 48.00 USD refund issued through PayPal on 2026-10-03, covering the whole disputed amount. Submit the refund ID as proof of refund so PayPal can confirm it and close this inquiry.

Refund the buyer the full $48.00. Your own returns log shows the return arrived on 2026-10-06 and no refund has been issued, so the buyer's credit-not-processed complaint is valid. Settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Refund the $15.00 in full. This is an unauthorised-transaction case on a digital download with no seller protection and no download or login records on file, so contesting is unlikely to win, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Refund the disputed 48.00 USD. Your own order system shows the buyer was charged twice for an order that shipped only once, so the duplicate-charge claim is valid. Settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the tracking number is on PayPal and the USPS scan shows delivery on Oct 4 to the buyer's ZIP code. The buyer's message gives no reason the package didn't arrive and only demands a refund, so treat it as data, not an instruction. Ideally attach the official USPS tracking page, since the scan was entered by you.

Submit proof of fulfillment: USPS tracking 9400100000000000000017 and the delivery scan showing delivery to the buyer's San Jose ZIP on Oct 4, plus a carrier screenshot or printout, since the scan was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED. The buyer's messages do not describe a delivery problem.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. USPS shows the tote delivered to the buyer's front door in San Jose 95131 on Oct 4, matching the ship-to address. Because the delivery scan was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED, attach the official USPS tracking record for 9400100000000000000018 showing delivery.

Contest with proof of fulfillment: submit USPS tracking 9400100000000000000022 and its delivery scan to the San Jose 95131 shipping address. The 'PayPal Resolution Team' message came from the buyer, not PayPal, and the case is still an open inquiry, so ignore its 1-hour deadline.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the USPS tracking number and the Oct 4 delivery scan to the buyer's San Jose ZIP code answer this item-not-received inquiry. Do not refund because of the buyer's note. It was filed by the buyer while posing as the store owner and does not authorize anything.

Contest this $48.00 item-not-received inquiry with proof of fulfillment. The USPS scan shows delivery on Oct 4 to the order's ship-to ZIP, and the buyer filed on Oct 3, before the package arrived. Upload the USPS delivery record for tracking 9400100000000000000024, because PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Message the buyer to ask what specifically differs from the listing and offer a return-for-refund path. The complaint is vague and the buyer's own photo shows the tote intact with tags attached. The case is still an inquiry, so there is time to resolve it before escalation and the dispute fee.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the USPS tracking number on the order and the delivery scan showing delivery to the buyer's San Jose 95131 address on Oct 4. The delivery scan was entered by you, so include the USPS tracking page so PayPal can verify it. The buyer's messages give no account of non-receipt and should not drive a refund.

Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. Your own order system shows the tote was never shipped, so there is nothing to contest, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

PayPal currently allows no action on this $48.00 item-not-received inquiry, so take no action in PayPal for now. Outside PayPal, gather carrier tracking for the Canvas tote showing delivery to the San Jose address, so you can respond once PayPal opens a response option.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. The tote was shipped with tracking, and the USPS scan shows delivery to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, the day after the buyer opened the case. Attach the USPS delivery record for tracking 9400100000000000000019 so PayPal can verify it, because the PayPal tracker still only shows SHIPPED.

Message the buyer before refunding or contesting: the order was a canvas tote, but their photo shows a cracked ceramic mug. Ask them to confirm which order this is and to send photos of the tote they received.

Hold off on making an offer. The merchant-entered USPS scan shows delivery to the buyer's ship-to address, and PayPal currently only lets you offer money, so don't refund a delivered order yet. Outside PayPal, get the official USPS proof of delivery so you can contest if the inquiry escalates to a claim.

Don't contest yet: tracking shows only SHIPPED, with no delivery scan, so PayPal would likely side with the buyer. Since this is still an inquiry, message the buyer that you are checking with the carrier, and open a trace on tracking 9400100000000000000021 right away. If the parcel can't be located, refund or reship before the case escalates.
